name: Mono
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Olson, Kenneth S. 2004. Mono. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 34(2): 233-238 (Illustrations of the IPA). doi:10.1017/S0025100304001744
catalog_locator: p. 236, section 'Tones'; p. 235 for 'Length and nasalization are not contrastive in Mono'
catalog_quote: Mono is a tone language with three tone levels, high /´/, mid /¯/, and low /`/. Rising and falling tones occur, but these are analyzed as sequences of level tones. H áwá 'diarrhea' M āwā 'road' L àwà 'fear' All possible combinations of level tones occur in monosyllabic, bisyllabic and trisyllabic words. As mentioned above, the tone on verbs varies depending on tense, aspect, and mood. Certain locative adverbs have a H–L–H tonal melody associated with them. The prepositional prefix /ga-/ exhibits tonal polarity; it bears an L tone if the prepositional root bears an H tone. It bears an H tone if the root bears either an M tone or an L tone.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mono is described as a three-level tone language (H, M, L; contours = tone sequences; lexical and grammatical tone). The open primary description says nothing about word stress or accent; no stress position can be extracted. Length is stated to be non-contrastive (contour-bearing vowels are phonetically long per Olson 2005:44 as reported by Paster 2006).
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Tonal: H-L-H melody on some locative adverbs; polarity on prefix ga-.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone illustrated on citation forms and a read passage (Bili dialect). No phrase-level prominence discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: All Olson sources describe the Bili dialect of Mono (Bosobolo Zone, Equateur, DRC), which speakers regard as the prestige variety; glottocode mono1270 (language level). Not to be confused with Mono of Cameroon (mono1269), Mono-Alu (mono1273) or Mono/Monachi of California (mono1275).

new_statements.quote: The majority of African languages have tonal systems, and Mono is no exception. Mono has three contrastive level tones: High (H, marked with an acute accent above the vowel), Mid (M, marked with a macron above the vowel), and Low (L, marked with a grave accent). Rising and falling contour tones also exist in the language, but I analyze them as sequences of level tones as discussed below. Tone carries both lexical and grammatical function in Mono.

new_statements.relation_note: Same author, same analysis as the catalog record (Olson 2004 JIPA: 'Mono is a tone language with three tone levels.. Rising and falling tones.. analyzed as sequences of level tones'): tonal, no word-stress statement. Adds nothing on stress; the 2005 book text itself is still unopened, but its held review (Paster 2006) shows the same chapter plan and never uses the word 'stress'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mono (Bili dialect) is described as a tone language with three contrastive level tones (High, Mid, Low); rising and falling contours are analysed as sequences of level tones; tone has lexical and grammatical (TAM) function, with a tonal melody on certain locative adverbs and tonal polarity on the prepositional prefix ga-. The dissertation has chapters on phonemes, tone, labialization/palatalization, the syllable ((C)(G)V; contour tones lengthen vowels), word shapes (bisyllabic minimality, augmentation, echo-vowel epenthesis), morphology and acoustic phonetics, and nowhere states anything about word stress or accent in Mono: the only occurrence of 'stress' (p.76) concerns Selayarese (Goldsmith 1990) in a comparison about epenthetic vowels.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none: no stress of any degree is described for Mono
new_statements.exceptions: none regarding stress; tonal specifics only (LH rising tone rare; vowels under contour tones phonetically long; H-L-H melody on some locative adverbs; polarity of ga-)
new_statements.identity_note: Olson's works (2001 dissertation, 2004 JIPA, 2005 book) describe the Bili dialect of Mono, a Banda (Ubangi) language of northwestern DR Congo (ISO 639-3 mnh), not the Uto-Aztecan Mono of California nor Mono-Alu of the Solomons.

sources.note: Second-hand chapter-by-chapter summary of Olson 2005 (Introduction, Phonemes, Tone, Labialization & Palatalization, Syllable, Word Shapes, Morphology, Acoustic Phonetics). Reports three-way tonal contrast H/M/L, contour tones on phonetically long vowels (Olson p.44), (C)(G)V syllable, bimoraic word-minimality repairs; the word 'stress' does not occur in the review.
'It is a tonal language.' No stress statement (tertiary).
